title: What reliable should mean for LLMs in life sciences
excerpt: Reliable life-science answers need bounded claims, source-linked evidence, explicit uncertainty, and repeatable evaluation.

pageSections.title: Reliability in life sciences is a systems property, not a tone of voice
pageSections.description: A response does not become reliable because it sounds careful. It becomes more reliable when the surrounding system constrains what can be claimed, preserves the evidence in scope, and makes later checking possible.
pageSections.context: That is why the discussion has to move away from stylistic fluency and toward architecture, provenance, and evaluation.

pageSections.title: Reliability is not a style attribute
pageSections.description: The hardest failure is not awkward wording. It is unsupported confidence.
pageSections.markdown:
In life sciences and other regulated domains, reliability requires bounded claims, visible evidence, and language proportionate to the source material.

The surrounding system must let a reviewer check the answer, narrow its scope, and trace it back to the material that supports it.

pageSections.eyebrow: What the system has to do
pageSections.title: A more serious definition of reliability has four parts
pageSections.description: These are not interface flourishes. They are operational requirements.

items.label: Evidence
items.title: The source material has to remain present
items.body: If the answer cannot be read against the documents, passages, or records that support it, later review becomes speculative.

items.label: Constraint
items.title: The claim has to stay inside its scope
items.body: Useful systems limit each claim to the scope supported by available evidence.

items.label: Uncertainty
items.title: The limits have to remain visible
items.body: A technically serious answer states unresolved ambiguity explicitly.

items.label: Audit
items.title: The result has to be testable afterward
items.body: Reliability is not established at generation time alone. It has to survive inspection and comparison.

pageSections.title: Fluency creates a dangerous kind of confidence
pageSections.description: The system can sound coherent long before it is actually dependable.
pageSections.markdown:
The most important failure in these settings is rarely clumsy wording. The real risk is persuasive language that outruns its evidence. A model can produce a coherent explanation, a plausible summary, or a seemingly careful recommendation while still making unsupported or overstated claims.

Evaluation belongs at the center of the product. The system needs to record the available evidence, constrain each claim to that evidence, and keep uncertainty explicit.

pageSections.title: Evidence needs a durable place in the workflow
pageSections.description: Refract keeps documents, saved evidence, comparisons, and later analysis in one session record.
pageSections.markdown:
Refract treats context preservation as a product requirement. Reading, evidence capture, comparison, and later analysis remain attached to the same working session, keeping each claim close to the source material meant to justify it.

Reliability improves when the system makes sources, transformations, and limits easy to inspect.

pageSections.title: Grounding should be treated as part of the output
pageSections.description: Every answer should preserve the link between each claim and its supporting source.
pageSections.markdown:
A reliable life-science system should build the connection between response and evidence into its normal workflow. It should preserve source material, surface supporting excerpts, constrain generalization, and record how a conclusion was formed.

These controls give reviewers a practical way to check the system's output and define where it should stop.

pageSections.title: The more useful system is usually the more restrained one
pageSections.description: That is an honest tradeoff, not a marketing compromise.
pageSections.markdown:
A trustworthy life-science system shows why it produced a claim, which evidence supports it, and where the answer stops.

Evidence, scope, and provenance cannot compensate for weak data, validation, or scientific framing. The interface must preserve the information reviewers need to check those foundations.
